books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, A. The Second Two-Party System: The Democrats and the Whigs

stimulus.text: In November 1832, a South Carolina convention declared the federal tariff acts of 1828 and 1832 null and void inside the state. President Andrew Jackson answered in a proclamation on December 10, 1832: 'The Constitution of the United States forms a government, not a league... I consider the power to annul a law of the United States incompatible with the existence of the Union, contradicted expressly by the letter of the Constitution, and destructive of the great object for which it was formed.' In a Senate debate in January 1830, Daniel Webster had closed with the words: 'Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!'
stimulus.source_note: Quotations: Andrew Jackson, Proclamation on Nullification, December 10, 1832, and Daniel Webster, Second Reply to Hayne, January 26, 1830. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: How did the nullification crisis end without South Carolina leaving the Union?

options.text: Jackson sent federal troops to occupy Charleston and collect the tariff
options.misconception: Jackson the general sounds ready to march, so it is easy to think troops settled the crisis.

options.text: Congress paired the Force Bill with a compromise tariff that lowered rates
The Supreme Court struck down the tariff of 1828 as unconstitutional
options.misconception: Courts settle constitutional fights, so it is easy to credit the Supreme Court with ending this one.

options.text: South Carolina repealed its ordinance before Jackson could respond at all
options.misconception: A crisis that ends peacefully invites the thought that one side simply backed down first.

rationales.A: Jackson threatened force and prepared troops, but no federal army occupied Charleston; the compromise arrived before any fighting.
rationales.B: On March 2, 1833, Congress passed both the Force Bill, backing Jackson with force, and a compromise tariff cutting rates to 20 percent by 1842.
rationales.C: The Court never struck down the tariff; the crisis was settled by Congress, not by a court ruling.
rationales.D: South Carolina held its ground until the compromise passed, then nullified the Force Bill itself as a final gesture.
rationales.general:
1. See both halves of the settlement. Congress armed Jackson with the Force Bill and cut the tariff in the same stroke.
2. Ask why both halves mattered. Force alone would have meant war; a lower tariff alone would have rewarded defiance.
Background: both measures passed on March 2, 1833, letting each side claim a win.
Remember: a crisis that ends in compromise usually has two laws, not one — find the pair.
